note: Red-team corpus for the verifier (S6). Owned by the spec, not by the implementation. 'rejected' attacks must be refused before execution with the given diagnostic; 'contained' programs are accepted, and must then run to completion inside the proven bound with the given adversarial arguments as their only gas budget. The five entries marked regression are holes that existed in v0.1 and are now closed — they are the reason this file exists.

attacks.why: The caller's bound must carry the callee's loop cost with the argument substituted. Unsubstituted, the term belonged to a parameter the caller does not have, instantiate read it as zero, and the bound came out at 43 gas for a program that spends ~13000.
Two calls with the same symbolic argument must add, not share, a bound.
Substitution has to compose through a chain; a bound that survives one hop can still leak at the second.
The argument is a linear expression in a parameter, so its value form is 2n and the callee's coefficient doubles.
n - 1 can be negative; the value form has to bound the magnitude, not the signed value, or a negative argument shrinks the bound.
The body is charged once, so it has to be priced for the worst iteration. Pricing it with the first iteration's constant let g(0) stand in for every g(i).
An argument that shrinks as the counter grows must still be priced at its largest magnitude over the proven counter range.
After the loop the counter is unknown, so there is no argument form to substitute and no bound to publish. Refusing beats pricing g(9) as g(0).
Builtins are not free; sqrt/max/min have fixed costs that must be charged per iteration.
The bound assumes every iteration runs; an early exit can only spend less.
`<=` runs one iteration more than `<`; an off-by-one here is an out-of-gas trap on the last iteration.
Descending counters are a different arithmetic path; the trip count is (start - limit) / |step|.
`>= 0` includes the final zero iteration.
Assuming the counter starts at zero undercounts whenever it starts higher.
A step larger than one divides the trip count; ceiling vs floor decides the last partial iteration.
`4 > i` is `i < 4`; a verifier that only reads the left operand as the counter misses it and must not silently accept.
A step in both arms is guaranteed progress; the corpus also checks the verifier is not so strict that it rejects every branch at all.
Nested trip counts multiply; adding them halves the bound and traps at half the work.
Callee cost inside the inner loop is charged once per inner iteration, which is itself inside the outer product.
Array parameters are handles, not numbers: substitution must not demand a numeric form for them.
When the branch is not taken the loop makes no progress. A checker that looks for a step anywhere in the body accepts this and then proofs nothing.
One arm steps by one and the other by two: progress is not uniform, so no single step describes the body.
Two steps that cancel. The old analysis took the first assignment it found and declared progress; the loop never moves.
The else arm resets the counter, so a single step per iteration does not bound the loop.
The outer counter is advanced by the inner loop, so its value after one outer iteration is not a constant.
i = i * 2 is progress, but it is not a constant step and the trip count is logarithmic, not linear.
< with i = i - 1 moves away from the exit.
> with i = i + 1 moves away from the exit, and overflows instead of terminating.
A step of zero is a constant step by a naive reading and no progress at all by the real one.
A let inside the body shadows the counter; the outer variable is never advanced.
`while flag` has no counter and no limit; refusing it is the whole point of the default.
i starts at an arbitrary argument, so the trip count is not expressible as a linear form over the parameters.
Every iteration allocates and nothing frees; the bound scales with n, so for large n the arena runs out mid-run even though the gas proof held.
Fully constant, so no instantiation is needed to see it: 100 x 4095 f64 is 3.2 MB in a 1 MiB arena.
The callee's allocation has to be substituted and then multiplied by the caller's trip count; charging it once would pass.
Handles encode the length modulo 4096, so a longer array cannot be named at all.
n is bounded by nothing, so a[n] can read another array's slots in the arena. This is a memory-disclosure hole, not just a bounds bug.
An index expression has no proven range even when a variable near it does; the rule is about the expression, not its parts.
The counter is proven to reach 7 while the array has 4 slots; a loop bound is not an index bound.
After the loop the counter is exactly len, and every later read through it is out of bounds.
Step two visits 0 and 2; the proven range [0, 3] is wider than the visited set and must still be inside the array.
A descending counter has a range too, and it must include the final iteration.
Nested loops need both frames visible; the inner counter's range must not hide the outer one.
A variable that still holds a literal is as good as the literal; rejecting it would be needless precision loss.
The call graph must be acyclic; a recursive call has no verified cost to charge.
Two functions calling each other is still a cycle; per-function verification cannot resolve it.
The cycle is longer than two hops; the check has to follow the whole graph, not just direct self-calls.
Constant indices are checked by the typechecker; 8 is past the end of a four-element array.
